articles.body: When you add Pay by Bank to a checkout, you call one endpoint. Your provider gives you a link, the customer taps it, picks their bank, approves, and comes back. Done. At the bank end, that one tap is about six API calls. And the bank isn't one you picked. Your customer picked it. If they bank with someone whose API has a rough night, that's your checkout having a rough night. I run engineering at a payment initiation provider, so those six calls are what my team works on every day. Here's what they are, and what the latest public numbers say about the banks behind them. The six calls This is the UK Open Banking flow for a single domestic payment. Names are from v3.1 of the spec, which is what most banks still expose.

articles.title: Why LLM latency grows with conversation length, and the measured fix: a flat 0.1605 s to 0.1651 s step over 20,000 steps
articles.excerpt: LLM latency grows with conversation length because the prompt the model must read grows with it. If the host holds the state and shows the model the exact state instead of the history, the prompt stay…
articles.body: LLM latency grows with conversation length because the prompt the model must read grows with it. If the host holds the state and shows the model the exact state instead of the history, the prompt stays the size of the state and the step time stays flat. Measured: a step took 0.1605 s early and 0.1651 s late (+2.8 percent) over 20,000 steps on a 7B model, with the prompt near 620 tokens throughout. Naming note: "AXI" here is the AXI host-side runtime for LLM agents, an architecture by Rajnish Choubey. It is not the ARM AMBA AXI chip-bus protocol. Why does latency rise as a conversation gets longer? Before the first output token the model reads the prompt.

articles.title: LLM agent token cost: why a kept chat grows with the square of the steps, and the measured fix (prompt caching counted)
articles.excerpt: An agent that keeps its whole chat resends everything on every step, so the tokens it sends grow with the square of the number of steps. Holding the state on the host and showing the model the exact s…
articles.body: An agent that keeps its whole chat resends everything on every step, so the tokens it sends grow with the square of the number of steps. Holding the state on the host and showing the model the exact state keeps the prompt the size of the state. Measured on Gemini 3.8 Flash: 85 times fewer prompt tokens a step and 76 times fewer in all over 400 turns, and 4.5 times lower cost per step that ends with the right state. Naming note: "AXI" here is the AXI host-side runtime for LLM agents, an architecture by Rajnish Choubey. It is not the ARM AMBA AXI chip-bus protocol. Why does the token bill of a chat-based agent grow so fast? If step t sends a prompt of a + b·t tokens (the fixed part plus everything said so far), n steps send n·a + b·n(n+1)/2 tokens in all.

articles.title: I built shadcn/ui for Angular 22: install it or own the source
articles.excerpt: React developers have had shadcn/ui for a while: good-looking components, accessible by default, and code you own. I work in Angular, and I wanted the same thing for Angular. Same classes, same varian…
articles.body: React developers have had shadcn/ui for a while: good-looking components, accessible by default, and code you own. I work in Angular, and I wanted the same thing for Angular. Same classes, same variants, same feel, and current Angular, not something ported from an older version. I couldn't find a close match, so I built it. It's called Ivorie , it's MIT, and version 1.4 is on npm today. This post shows what it does with real code you can paste. Repo: https://github.com/Inlaylab/ivorie Docs and playground: https://inlaylab.github.io/ivorie/ Ivorie is an independent project. It's not affiliated with shadcn/ui. It ports shadcn/ui's design (MIT) to Angular, with credit. What you get 53 components with the shadcn/ui look and behavior. Keyboard and ARIA follow Radix patterns. Angular 22 only.

articles.body: “Nightmare at 20,000 Feet” is one of the all-time great episodes of The Twilight Zone . Starring William Shatner, the story is about a man who is taking his first flight after having had a nervous breakdown. During the flight, he looks out the window and sees a creature, called a gremlin, on the wing that taunts him and tears apart pieces of the plane. No one can see the gremlin but him, and even his own wife attributes it to his fragile mental state. The story is a brilliant commentary on paranoia and Shatner was captivating in the role. It was so good that it sometimes overshadows Shatner’s other great episode of The Twilight Zone , which premiered 66 years ago today.

articles.body: Hundreds of websites using the Optimizely website personalization platform served unsuspecting visitors a potent malware cocktail that targeted cryptocurrency wallets, stole payment card data, cookies, and screenshots, and delivered exploit kits for infecting iPhones and iPads, researchers said Tuesday. ReportURI said it identified 178 websites—including CNN, Zoom, the BBC, and Salesforce—that were affected. JavaScript digitally signed by Optimizely and then loaded into customer pages had been modified to include malicious components that attempted to infect visitor devices with multiple payloads. When wares were installed successfully, they swapped user cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attackers.

articles.title: NASA's Voyager 1 launched second, so how did it beat Voyager 2 to a light-day by nearly a decade?
articles.excerpt: Voyager 1 just reached a light-day in space, but Voyager 2 won't do the same until 2035, due to speed choices made throughout their 50-year missions.
articles.body: Voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035. Why the big difference? On Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will be so far away from Earth that it will take a full light-day (24 hours) to send a signal to the distant spacecraft, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal — so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky. But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer?

NASA On Nov. 14 and 15, NASA held the annual Space Apps Challenge with a record-breaking 181,835 registered participants taking part in 593 events around the world. The annual hackathon invites participants to use NASA’s open data to address one of 14 challenges focused on space exploration or Earth science. This year, the hackathon drew 59% more registrants and was the 5th year in a row with increased participation. Since 2012, NASA Space Apps Challenge has hosted the two-day event, which has included more than 600,000 people from more than 190 countries.

articles.title: Space is filling up with junk. Could laser-reflecting mirrors help humanity clean things up?
articles.excerpt: The British company Foundational thinks its laser-reflecting tech can help humanity fight the space-junk problem — and it just proved out a demo version in an orbital test.
articles.body: A British startup thinks it can help humanity deal with its space junk problem. Millions of pieces of space debris circle Earth at the moment, according to the European Space Agency (ESA). Even the smallest fragments are potentially dangerous, given how fast stuff travels in orbit. Experts have proposed a range of measures to deal with this junk. The smallest bits, for example, may require big space nets, or lasering the stuff down to Earth. Large satellites are increasingly being deliberately deorbited these days, and a few have even been refueled to keep them operating in orbit — something that will likely start happening more and more over the coming years. Now, the British startup Foundational has another idea to throw into the mix: retroreflectors.

Four new sonifications use data of stars that are actively forming, captured by Chandra and other NASA telescopes By studying places in the universe where stars are currently being born and young stars are present, astronomers can better understand the lifecycle of all stars, including our own Sun. articles.excerpt: Hack into our handy guide to this electrifying adaptation of William Gibson’s cult ‘80s novel.
articles.body: We're in a bit of a cyberpunk revival at the moment. 2026 gave the excellent second season of Netflix’s "Cyberpunk: Edgerunners," and Prime Video's " Blade Runner 2099 " is just around the corner. 2027 will continue this trend with " Neuromancer " blasting onto Apple TV. Based on cyberspace guru William Gibson’s seminal 1984 novel, "Neuromancer" follows Case, a brilliant hacker who falls into a web of digital espionage and crime as he attempts an impossible corporate heist. The pulp noir novel has been hailed as a generational revelation, and its slang and terminology have become ingrained in computer nerd subcultures.
